strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 23 setups with 6 SOTA attacks, 9 architectures, and multiple datasets; rigorous adherence to prior protocols ensures fair comparison with existing defenses like BiDO
Strong empirical results, especially on high-resolution images (224×224), achieving both better attack accuracy and higher natural accuracy than prior defenses simultaneously
Simple, practical method requiring only a single hyperparameter (ah=0.4) that is easy to implement and integrate into existing training pipelines without modifying standard objectives
Consistent improvements across diverse settings (white-box and label-only attacks, multiple architectures and datasets) demonstrate robustness of the approach
Well-designed ablation studies on masking values and area ratios; user study with 300 votes provides perceptual validation; thorough supplementary material supports reproducibility
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Fig. 1 and 2) that clearly convey the privacy-utility tradeoff
weaknesses: Weak theoretical justification: the core claim that 'MI attacks require significant private information' is stated intuitively but never rigorously formalized; Section 2.2 demonstrates that RE works empirically but provides no principled explanation for why masking reduces attack accuracy more than classification accuracy

No discussion of adaptive attacks or robustness to informed adversaries—if attackers know the defense mechanism, they could train with RE or adapt their reconstruction strategy, but this vulnerability is not addressed

Limited novelty: the method directly applies existing random erasing from data augmentation literature [32] with minimal conceptual innovation; the contribution is primarily empirical validation of an intuitive idea rather than new methodology or theory

Hyperparameter generalization concerns: ah=0.4 is claimed as universally fixed but was selected based on a single setup (Table 7, PLGMI/FaceNet64); ablation tested only one attack method; no sensitivity analysis across all 23 setups raises questions about true generality

User study is inconclusive: only ~2% difference between BiDO (153/300) and MIDRE (147/300) votes; single setup coverage (PLGMI/VGG16/CelebA) limits generalization; marginal differences could be within noise

Overclaimed results: 'SOTA performance' is setup and metric dependent; on VGG16 (Table 2) MIDRE achieves identical natural accuracy to BiDO (79.85%) despite lower attack accuracy; claims of being 'first' on 224×224 need more context

Speculative interpretation of GRADCAM results (Appendix B.2): claims that models learn 'partial information' lack rigorous validation and could represent exploitable vulnerabilities rather than defensive properties

Missing information-theoretic analysis: no formal analysis of mutual information reduction or what constitutes 'significant' information; evaluation relies only on empirical metrics without theoretical grounding

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 23 setups with 6 SOTA attacks, 9 architectures, multiple datasets, and resolutions (64×64 and 224×224), including user studies and thorough ablation studies
Practical simplicity: requires only one hyperparameter with no expensive grid search, unlike BiDO; trivial to implement and complementary to existing defenses
Interesting and noteworthy result at high resolution (224×224) where MIDRE improves natural accuracy while reducing attack accuracy by 40-45%
Strong and consistent empirical results showing 30-70% attack accuracy reduction with moderate 5-7% natural accuracy drops across most setups
Detailed supplementary materials with ablation studies on masking values, area ratios, GRADCAM visualizations, and likelihood distributions
weaknesses: Limited novelty: applies an existing technique (random erasing from [32]) to a new problem without developing new conceptual understanding or methodological innovation

Lack of rigorous theoretical analysis: Section 2.2 provides only empirical observation rather than mechanistic explanation; the central claim that 'MI attacks require private information' is asserted without formal validation or information-theoretic analysis

Fundamental unaddressed question: does training with RE produce the same decision boundary as unmasked training? If different, the model solves a different problem and 'natural accuracy' comparisons are misleading; if same, the mechanism for preventing MI is unclear

Problematic evaluation methodology: relies on a separate 'evaluation model' to assess reconstructed image quality without critically justifying this approach or analyzing sensitivity to evaluation model choice; potential circular reasoning when evaluation model is trained on masked private data

Hyperparameter consistency issue: fixes a_h=0.4 across all 23 setups based on single setup ablation (PLGMI, FaceNet64); no evidence this is optimal for all scenarios; contradicts the criticism that BiDO requires grid search

Concerning GRADCAM analysis (Supplementary B.2) reveals RE-trained models have 'focused' attention requiring only partial information, suggesting they learn from incomplete data; unclear if this represents a genuine privacy advantage or exploitable vulnerability
Limited scope: all experiments restricted to face recognition and classification; generalization to medical imaging, NLP, other domains, or model types (regression, generation) is unexplored

Missing critical baselines: no comparison with differential privacy defenses [49,50], GAN-based defenses [51], or other simple augmentation techniques (Gaussian blur, crops, mixup); excuse of 'code not available' is insufficient
Weak user study validation: only 150 image pairs from 20 classes with marginal results (153 vs 147 out of 300 votes, ~2% difference) providing insufficient evidence of superiority

Insufficient statistical rigor: no formal significance testing between methods; some differences within error bars; no multiple comparison corrections across 23 setups; number of random seeds and variance computation not clearly specified

Suspicious result at high resolution (224×224): natural accuracy improves rather than degrades—contradicts proposed mechanism; unexplained and deserves investigation into whether this is regularization, generalization artifact, or other phenomenon

Fairness concerns in comparisons: paper reimplemented BiDO/MID but claims 'careful tuning' without showing sensitivity analysis or evidence equal effort was invested; only BiDO has pre-trained model provided by authors

strengths: Novel repurposing of random erasing from data augmentation to MI defense, with practical simplicity requiring only one hyperparameter (unlike BiDO's expensive grid search)
Comprehensive experimental validation: 23 setups across 6 SOTA attacks, 9 architectures including ViTs, 5 datasets, 2 resolutions, plus user study validation

Strong empirical results achieving SOTA privacy-utility tradeoffs: 43.74% reduction in attack accuracy vs. BiDO while maintaining comparable natural accuracy; first to improve natural accuracy (2.47-3.06%) at high resolution while reducing attacks 40-45%
Solid analytical support demonstrating RE degrades attack accuracy substantially (up to 72.69%) while affecting natural accuracy only moderately (0.45%)
Excellent presentation, clear algorithm, good reproducibility with detailed specifications and promised code availability
Well-designed ablation studies on masking values and area ratios that support the core findings
weaknesses: Limited theoretical foundation: core claim that MI attacks require private information is empirically validated but lacks formal justification; no information-theoretic analysis or formal privacy guarantees

Concerning defense mechanism: GRADCAM analysis reveals defense works partly by exploiting partial-information foolability rather than genuinely limiting information; reconstructed images can fool the model while lacking complete identity features, raising robustness concerns

Limited scope and generalization: experiments focus heavily on face recognition (CelebA, FaceScrub) with unclear applicability to other modalities (medical imaging, text, tabular data) where occlusion robustness may not apply
Incomplete comparisons: BiDO and MID re-implemented by authors without verification of implementation quality; no experiments combining MIDRE with existing defenses despite claims of complementarity

Evaluation metric limitations: attack accuracy uses evaluation model as proxy (distinct architecture, trained on private data); user study limited (150 pairs, single attack method); KNN metric still depends on representation quality

Insufficient ablation analysis: no explanation for why defense effectiveness varies dramatically across attacks (GMI nearly nullified at ae=0.3 but PLG-MI remains 93% at ae=0.2); limited exploration of lower bound (al=0.1); only three ah values tested
No evaluation against adaptive attacks specifically designed to exploit the partial-information vulnerability or attacks with knowledge of RE defense

Modest accuracy-privacy tradeoffs in some settings: 3-7% natural accuracy cost common; 40% attack success rate remains at recommended settings; unclear whether defense should be framed as heuristic or formal privacy approach

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 37 setups with multiple datasets, architectures, and SOTA MI attacks
Insightful feature space analysis demonstrating mechanistic understanding of why Random Erasing provides defense effectiveness
Systematic identification and validation of two key properties (Partial Erasure and Random Location) through controlled experiments
Strong empirical results showing superior privacy-utility trade-offs compared to existing MI defenses (NLS, TL-DWI, BiDO, etc.)
Includes user studies to validate attack effectiveness beyond automated metrics
Rigorous ablation studies examining masking strategies, masking values, area ratios, and adaptive attacks
Well-presented with effective visualizations and clear writing
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty - Random Erasing is an existing data augmentation technique; primary contribution is empirical application and post-hoc analysis rather than novel methodology
Lack of theoretical justification - no formal privacy analysis, differential privacy guarantees, or theoretical bounds on privacy-utility trade-offs
Severe domain limitation - all experiments exclusively on face recognition; generalization to other sensitive domains (medical imaging, NLP, etc.) unclear and unaddressed
Significant utility degradation in several cases - e.g., 7% accuracy drop in Setup 1; claims of 'small impact' not universally supported
Hyperparameter sensitivity - method requires careful tuning of α_e; no principled approach for practitioners to select values; different models/datasets may require different tuning
Incomplete adaptive attack evaluation - assumes attacker knows masking parameters; sophisticated attacks exploiting RE statistics not fully explored
Privacy quantification issues - relies on attack accuracy rather than formal privacy definitions; relationship between attack accuracy reduction and actual privacy preservation not established
Potential comparison fairness concerns - different baseline defenses use different training procedures; incomplete hyperparameter tuning for baselines
Missing computational cost analysis - no evaluation of training overhead or practical deployment considerations
Statistical reporting inconsistencies - not all results include standard deviations, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 37 setups spanning 7 state-of-the-art MI attacks, 11 architectures, 6 datasets, and multiple resolutions provide extensive empirical support
Practical applicability: The defense is simple to implement (just random erasing during training) and can be combined with existing defense mechanisms without major modifications
Thorough ablation studies: Systematic investigation of masking strategies, area ratios, and masking values provides good coverage of design space
Privacy-utility trade-offs: Results demonstrate improvements in privacy-utility balance compared to several baselines (NLS, BiDO) in standard threat models
Detailed feature space analysis: Visualization of why RE creates discrepancy between MI-reconstructed and private images (though explanations could be deeper)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: The core contribution is applying Random Erasing (Zhong et al. 2020), an existing data augmentation technique. No new methodology is introduced, only an application of existing work
Lack of theoretical grounding: No rigorous justification for why random erasing specifically defends against MI attacks. The mechanism is documented empirically but not explained theoretically

Critical flaw - Adaptive attacks inadequately addressed: Section D.5 shows adaptive attacks significantly reduce defense effectiveness (Setup 1: AttAcc 10.5% to 38.53% in Setup 2), yet this is relegated to appendix with insufficient discussion. The defense may be vulnerable to informed adversaries

Circular reasoning in defense analysis: Claims that 'discrepancy prevents attacks' but doesn't explain why models don't learn to focus on non-erased regions. Figure 3b shows concerning partial overlap in feature space
Non-standard evaluation metrics: The 'Trade-off value (Δ)' is non-standard; many table entries use undefined notation ('OP', inconsistent 'NA' usage) making reproducibility difficult
Framing mismatch: Title questions 'Promising Defense or False Hope?' but paper doesn't adequately address the 'False Hope' possibility despite adaptive attack results suggesting exactly that

Insufficient conceptual contribution: Defense appears to be 'data corruption to obscure information' rather than principled privacy protection; conceptual difference from noise injection is never discussed
User study limitations: Only 450 total votes with subjective results contradicting metrics (221 for BiDO vs 108 for MIDRE); relegated to appendix without adequate discussion
Hyperparameter selection unclear: Uses α_e = 0.4 or 0.8 without principled justification; limited guidance for practitioners on parameter selection
Missing practical considerations: No discussion of computational overhead, scalability to large models, or applicability beyond face recognition

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across 7 SOTA MI attacks, 11 model architectures, and 6 datasets with multiple resolutions, demonstrating broad applicability of the proposed MIDRE defense
Novel feature space analysis (Section 3.2-3.3 with t-SNE visualizations) provides clear mechanistic understanding of why random erasing is effective as a privacy defense
Achieves state-of-the-art privacy-utility trade-offs, being the first to demonstrate competitive MI robustness without degrading natural accuracy at high-resolution (224×224 images)
Simplicity and practical applicability: method requires only a single hyperparameter (α) and can be easily integrated into standard training pipelines
Thorough ablation studies (Appendix D) systematically investigate design choices (masking strategies, values, area ratios, aspect ratios, adaptive attacks)
User study validation (Tables B.11-B.12) provides human-level confirmation of defense effectiveness through Amazon Mechanical Turk studies
Clear presentation with well-designed figures (especially Figures 1-3, 5-7) effectively communicating methodology and results
Extensive additional experiments and analysis in appendix (37 total setups) provide valuable benchmarks and insights for the community
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: random erasing is a well-established data augmentation technique (Zhong et al. 2020); the contribution is primarily applying it as a defense and analyzing why it works rather than developing fundamentally new methods

Lack of formal theoretical analysis: the three identified properties (P1: Partial Erasure, P2: Random Location, P3: Utility Recovery) are discovered empirically but lack rigorous mathematical justification or guarantees

Adaptive attack analysis is limited: the adaptive attacker (Section D.5) assumes knowledge only of the masking ratio α; more sophisticated adversaries aware of the defense mechanism could potentially devise better strategies

Hyperparameter selection guidance is incomplete: the choice of α=0.4 (low-res) and α∈{0.4, 0.8} (high-res) appears dataset and attack-dependent, with limited guidance for practitioners selecting parameters for new domains
Primary focus on vision/face recognition domain: generalization to other modalities (NLP, tabular data, graphs, time-series) remains unexplored, limiting broader applicability

Trade-off magnitude varies significantly: while high-resolution with small masking shows minimal utility loss, some configurations show 5-15% accuracy degradation, and the paper's claims about 'no utility sacrifice' are somewhat overstated
The adaptive attack evaluation remains relatively simple; the paper lacks analysis of whether more sophisticated adaptive attacks exploiting knowledge of the RE strategy could be developed
Computational overhead not explicitly discussed, though likely minimal for an augmentation-based approach
Some notational overloading (α used for multiple purposes) and occasional clarity issues (e.g., small Figure 3 visualizations)
